name: Purikura (大头贴)
blurb: Japanese photo sticker booths that print a sheet of tiny decorated selfies
title: What Is Purikura? Photo Sticker Booths in Japan and China
description: Purikura are photo sticker booths: pose in a cubicle, add frames and doodles, and get a sheet of tiny stickers. Launched in Japan in 1995, popular across Asia.
answer: Purikura are photo sticker booths: you step into a curtained cubicle, take a few photos, decorate them with frames and graphics, and a few minutes later the machine prints a sheet of small sticker photos. The first one, Print Club (プリント倶楽部), was made by the Japanese game company Atlus with Sega and launched in July 1995 at 300 yen a play. The booths spread across Asia; in China, where they are called datoutie (大头贴, big-head stickers), they arrived around 2000, faded as phone selfies took over, and came back in fashion around 2024.

body: Booths stood in arcades, malls and shopping streets, their curtains covered with sample photos of smiling models. Inside you posed in front of a screen while the machine took a short burst of shots, then picked frames, backgrounds and cartoon stickers, and on many machines wrote on the pictures. Out came a sheet of adhesive photo paper divided into small frames, which you cut up and stuck on notebooks, pencil cases and phones.

Chinese reports from 2024 recall that early machines in China came with a paper catalogue: you chose an effect and frame in the book, typed its number into the machine and then shot. The usual remembered price was about 5 yuan a sheet.

body: Purikura is short for Print Club and became the everyday Japanese word for every brand of booth. In Chinese the name datoutie comes from the close-up, big-head look of the photos.

Yes. In Japan the number of booths fell from more than 50,000 in 1997 to about 11,000 by 2016, according to industry figures, but several companies still make new machines and taking purikura remains a normal outing for Japanese teenagers. In China the booths largely vanished in the 2010s, then reappeared in malls around 2024; newer machines usually send a digital copy to your phone as well as printing the stickers.

faq.a: The Japanese game company Atlus, working with Sega. Their Print Club machine launched in July 1995.
It is the Chinese name for photo sticker booths and their prints, literally big-head stickers, after the close-up shots.

faq.q: Can you still use purikura booths?
faq.a: Yes. They are still common in Japan, and in China they made a comeback around 2024.
